title: How to sell your motorcycle: prepare it, price it and close the deal
alt: A clean yellow and black motorcycle parked by the kerb on a quiet sunny street in front of a brick house
excerpt: A little preparation can add real money to your sale price and make the whole process faster. Here is how to get your motorcycle ready to sell, set a fair price and hand it over safely.

body.p: Selling a motorcycle privately usually gets you a better price than trading it in, but only if you put in some work first. Buyers judge a bike in the first few minutes, and a tidy machine with a clear history sells faster and for more than a neglected one with the same mileage. Here is how to give yours the best chance.
You do not need to restore the bike, but fixing obvious niggles costs little and removes reasons for buyers to haggle:

ul: Clean and lube the chain and check its adjustment, following our guide to [chain maintenance](/blog/motorcycle-chain-maintenance)
Check tyre pressures and tread depth, since worn tyres are an easy reason to knock money off
Make sure every light, indicator and the horn works
Replace cracked mirrors, missing bolts and tatty grips
Top up fluids and make sure the battery is charged so it starts first time

body.p: If a service is due soon, it is often worth doing it before you list the bike. A fresh service stamp is a strong selling point.

Put together the registration documents, spare keys, owner's manual and every receipt you can find. A complete record of services and repairs is one of the best ways to justify your asking price, as we explain in [why service history matters for resale value](/blog/service-history-motorcycle-resale-value). Buyers trust a bike more when they can see what has been done and when.

body.h: Clean it properly and take good photos

body.p: Wash the bike thoroughly, including the wheels and engine, and photograph it in daylight against a plain background. Take shots from both sides, the front and back, the dashboard showing the mileage, the tyres and any marks or damage. Being upfront about flaws builds trust and saves wasted viewings.

Look at listings for the same model, year and similar mileage, and note what they actually sell for rather than what people ask. Bikes with low mileage, a full history and recent work on tyres or chain can sit at the top of the range. Leave a little room for negotiation, since most buyers expect to talk the price down a bit.

Arrange viewings at your home or a public place during the day, and do not hand over keys for a test ride until you are happy. Many sellers ask for the full price in cash or a cleared payment before any test ride, or ask the buyer to hold a licence and insurance. Expect buyers to go through a checklist like our [used motorcycle buying checklist](/blog/buying-a-used-motorcycle-checklist), so go through it yourself first and you will not be caught off guard.

Only release the bike once payment has fully cleared. Write a simple receipt with both names, the date, the price, the mileage and the frame number, and keep a copy. Then notify the registration authority and cancel or transfer your insurance.

The easiest way to have a clean history ready on sale day is to keep it as you ride. MotoLog logs your mileage and services and reminds you when the next one is due soon or overdue, so you can get the app just below and start building that record now.

title: How to choose motorcycle boots
alt: A rider's tall black leather boot resting on the footboard of a large touring motorcycle, with chrome engine and wheel close up
excerpt: Your feet and ankles take a beating in even a minor fall. Here is what to look for in motorcycle boots, from protection and fit to waterproofing, so you buy a pair you will actually wear.

body.p: Boots are the piece of riding gear people most often skip. Plenty of riders who would never go out without a helmet will happily ride in trainers. The problem is that feet and ankles are among the most commonly injured parts of the body in motorcycle crashes, and even a simple drop at a junction can trap a foot under the bike. A good pair of boots is cheap insurance.
Motorcycle boots are built to do things everyday shoes cannot:

ul: Resist abrasion if you slide along the road
Stop the ankle from twisting or crushing under the weight of the bike
Protect the shin and ankle bones from impacts
Keep the sole stiff so your foot is not bent the wrong way
Stay on your feet in a crash, which laces alone often do not

body.p: Look for boots tested to the European standard EN 13634. The label shows ratings for height, abrasion resistance, impact cut resistance and transverse rigidity, with 2 being the higher level for each.
The best boot depends on how you ride:

ul: Touring boots are tall, usually waterproof and comfortable to walk in, which suits long days and trips
Sport boots are stiffer, with sliders and strong ankle bracing for fast road and track riding
Adventure boots combine tall protection with a grippy sole for gravel and off-road stops
Short urban boots and riding trainers look like normal shoes and are better than nothing, but offer less ankle and shin protection

body.p: Try boots on in the afternoon, when feet are slightly larger, and wear the socks you ride in. Your heel should not lift when you walk, and your toes should not touch the end. Then sit on a bike if you can. Check you can feel and work the gear lever easily, since a bulky toe box can make gear changes clumsy. As with [choosing gloves](/blog/how-to-choose-motorcycle-gloves), comfort matters: boots you dislike wearing tend to stay in the cupboard.

If you ride all year, a waterproof membrane is worth paying for. Wet feet get cold fast, and cold riders lose concentration. Our tips for [riding in the rain](/blog/how-to-ride-a-motorcycle-in-the-rain) cover the rest of a wet weather setup. In hot climates, a vented boot may suit you better, as long as it still has proper ankle protection.

Clean off road grime and salt after wet rides, let boots dry naturally away from direct heat, and treat leather now and then so it does not crack. Check soles, zips and buckles as part of your [pre-ride check](/blog/five-minute-pre-ride-check), and replace boots that have been through a crash, just as you would a [helmet after an impact](/blog/how-to-choose-a-motorcycle-helmet).

title: How to work out your motorcycle's fuel consumption
alt: A rider in a full-face helmet sitting on a motorcycle at a petrol station forecourt in warm evening light, with scooters at the pumps behind
excerpt: Knowing how far your bike goes on a tank helps you plan rides and spot problems early. Here is a simple way to measure your motorcycle's real fuel consumption and what to do if it gets worse.

body.p: Most riders have a rough idea of how far they get on a tank, but very few know the real number. That is a shame, because fuel consumption is one of the best early warnings you have. A bike that suddenly needs more fuel to cover the same distance is often telling you something needs attention, long before a warning light comes on.
The most reliable way to measure consumption needs nothing more than your odometer and a fuel receipt:

ul: Fill the tank to the same level every time, ideally at the same pump, and note the odometer reading
Ride normally until you next need fuel
Fill to the same level again and note how many litres it took and the new odometer reading
Divide the litres by the distance and multiply by 100 to get litres per 100 km

body.p: For example, if you rode 280 km and it took 14 litres to fill up again, that is 14 ÷ 280 × 100 = 5 litres per 100 km. If you prefer kilometres per litre, divide the distance by the litres instead: 280 ÷ 14 = 20 km per litre. Do this over three or four tanks and take the average, since a single fill can be thrown off by a short trip or a pump that clicks off early.

body.h: Why the dashboard figure is not enough

body.p: Many modern bikes show an average consumption figure, and it is useful for a quick check. But it is an estimate, and it can be optimistic by several percent. Working it out from real fill-ups gives you an honest baseline you can compare against over months and seasons. That is one more reason it pays to [track your mileage](/blog/why-track-motorcycle-mileage) properly rather than relying on memory.
Some changes are normal. Cold weather, heavy luggage, a passenger, motorway speeds and stop-start traffic will all push the figure up. If none of those explain it, look at the bike itself:

ul: Low tyre pressures add rolling resistance, so check them as part of your [tyre care routine](/blog/motorcycle-tyre-care-pressure-tread-and-age)
A dirty air filter makes the engine work harder, which our guide to [cleaning or replacing the air filter](/blog/motorcycle-air-filter-when-to-clean-or-replace) covers
A dry or tight chain wastes power between the engine and the rear wheel
Worn spark plugs or an overdue service can leave the engine running less efficiently
Dragging brakes, which you can often feel as warmth in the disc after a ride

body.h: Use it to plan your range

body.p: Once you know your real consumption and your tank size, you know your real range. Take that number, knock off a safety margin of around 20 percent, and you have a figure you can trust when [planning a longer trip](/blog/how-to-plan-a-motorcycle-trip) through areas where fuel stations are far apart.

MotoLog makes the first half of this easy: log your mileage at each fill-up and you will always have the distances to hand, along with reminders when a service is due soon or overdue. You can get the app just below.

title: Motorcycle air filter: when to clean or replace it
alt: A mechanic sitting on a stool beside a scooter engine and rear wheel stripped down on a workshop floor, with tools laid out in front
excerpt: A clogged air filter quietly costs you power and fuel. Here is how often to check your motorcycle's air filter, how to tell when it needs attention, and whether to clean or replace it.

body.p: The air filter is one of the easiest parts of a motorcycle to forget. It sits out of sight under the seat, tank or a side panel, and it rarely fails in a dramatic way. Instead, it slowly fills with dust, bugs and grime until the engine has to work harder for every breath. Looking after it is cheap, quick and one of the best things you can do for how your bike runs.

Your engine burns a mix of fuel and air, and it needs a lot of air. The filter stops dust and grit from being drawn into the engine, where it would wear the cylinders, piston rings and valves. A clean filter lets air through freely while catching the dirt. A blocked one restricts airflow, which can make the engine run rich, feel flat and use more fuel.

Most manufacturers list an air filter check or replacement every 10,000 to 20,000 km, or at set services. Your owner's manual has the exact figure, and our [service intervals cheat sheet](/blog/motorcycle-service-intervals-cheat-sheet) shows where it usually fits alongside oil, plugs and valves. Check more often if you:

ul: Ride on gravel, dirt or dusty roads
Spend a lot of time in heavy city traffic
Ride in areas with lots of pollen, sand or insects
Have just come back from a long trip on mixed roads

body.p: A dirty filter does not always announce itself, but there are clues. The bike may feel sluggish when you open the throttle, fuel economy may drop, or the engine may hesitate or run unevenly. Once you can get to the filter, look at it against the light. If it is dark, caked with dirt or you can barely see light through it, it is time to act.
It depends on the type of filter your bike uses:

ul: Paper filters are the most common on road bikes. They cannot be washed, so replace them when they are dirty. You can gently tap out loose dust between changes, but never blow compressed air through from the clean side or soak them.
Foam filters, common on off-road bikes, are washed in filter cleaner or warm soapy water, dried fully and re-oiled with proper foam filter oil.
Oiled cotton gauze filters are cleaned with a dedicated kit and lightly re-oiled. Too much oil can foul sensors, so follow the kit's instructions.

body.p: Whatever the type, make sure the filter seats properly and the airbox lid seals all the way round. A filter that lets air bypass it is worse than a dirty one. A few basic tools from a [rider's toolkit](/blog/basic-motorcycle-toolkit-every-rider-should-own) are usually all you need to get to it.

Because the air filter is checked so rarely, it is easy to lose track of when it was last done. Write down the date and the odometer reading each time you clean or replace it. A record like this also adds weight to your [service history when you sell](/blog/service-history-motorcycle-resale-value), since buyers like to see the small jobs were done too.
If you would rather not rely on memory, MotoLog can log your mileage and remind you when your next air filter check is due soon or overdue. You can get the app just below.

title: Motorcycle warning lights explained: what each one means
alt: A lit digital motorcycle instrument cluster at night showing neutral, the odometer and an amber oil warning light
excerpt: A light on the dash can mean anything from a reminder to a reason to stop right now. Here is what the common motorcycle warning lights mean and what to do about each one.

body.p: Modern motorcycles have more warning lights than ever, and it is not always obvious which ones matter. Some are simply information, some mean you should get the bike checked soon, and a few mean you should pull over as soon as it is safe. The exact symbols vary between manufacturers, so your owner's manual is the final word, but most bikes follow the same broad rules.
Colour is the quickest guide to how serious a light is:

ul: Green or blue lights are information, such as neutral, indicators or high beam
Amber or yellow lights mean something needs attention soon, but you can usually ride on carefully
Red lights mean stop as soon as it is safe and find out what is wrong

body.p: Usually red and shaped like an oil can. If it comes on while riding, stop as soon as you safely can and switch off the engine. Low oil pressure can destroy an engine in minutes. Check the oil level once the bike has stood for a few minutes, and do not ride on if the light stays on after topping up. Keeping to sensible [oil change intervals](/blog/how-often-change-motorcycle-oil) makes this far less likely.

Often red, with a thermometer symbol. It means the engine is running too hot. Stop, let it cool, and check the coolant level once the engine is cold. Never open a hot radiator cap. A temperature light in slow summer traffic can point to a cooling fan that is not switching on.

A red or amber battery symbol means the charging system is not keeping the battery topped up. The bike may run for a while on what is left in the battery, but it will eventually stop. Head home or to a garage by the shortest route, and turn off heated grips and other accessories to save power. Our guide to [motorcycle battery care](/blog/motorcycle-battery-care) explains how to test the battery afterwards.

The ABS light normally comes on when you switch on and goes out once you ride off. If it stays on, the anti-lock system may be switched off because of a fault, but the normal brakes still work. Ride gently, leave extra stopping room, and get it checked, along with a look at the [brake pads and fluid](/blog/motorcycle-brake-pads-and-fluid-when-to-replace).

Usually amber and shaped like an engine. It means the bike's computer has spotted a fault. If the bike runs normally you can usually ride on carefully and get it diagnosed soon. If it flashes, or the bike misfires or loses power, stop and get help.

Many bikes show a spanner symbol when a service is due based on time or mileage. It is not a fault, but it is easy to ignore until it becomes one. Our [service intervals cheat sheet](/blog/motorcycle-service-intervals-cheat-sheet) covers what each service usually includes.
If your bike has no service light, or you would like a reminder you can rely on, MotoLog tracks your mileage and tells you when each service is due soon or overdue. You can get the app just below.

title: How to pack a motorcycle for a weekend trip
alt: A black cruiser motorcycle with a brown leather saddlebag and a helmet on the seat, parked against a weathered concrete wall
excerpt: Packing a motorcycle is a balancing act, literally. Here is what to bring for a weekend away, how to carry it, and how to load the bike so it still handles well.

body.p: A weekend away is one of the best ways to enjoy a motorcycle, but you cannot just throw a suitcase in the boot. Space is tight, weight changes how the bike handles, and anything badly strapped down can work loose at speed. With a bit of planning, though, two or three days of kit fits easily on almost any bike.
The most common mistake is bringing too much. Lay out everything you plan to take, then put a third of it back. A weekend usually needs:

ul: One change of riding base layers and one set of casual clothes
Light shoes, so you are not walking around all evening in boots
A waterproof oversuit or rain layer, even if the forecast looks good
Toiletries in small travel bottles
Phone charger, a power bank and any cables for your intercom or sat nav
A small kit of tools, a puncture repair kit and a torch, ideally the [basic toolkit](/blog/basic-motorcycle-toolkit-every-rider-should-own) you already carry

body.p: Soft saddlebags, a tail bag and a tank bag cover most weekend trips and fit almost any bike. Hard panniers and top boxes are lockable and fully waterproof, but they need mounting racks. Whatever you use, line soft bags with dry bags or bin liners, because very few are truly waterproof in a long downpour. Keep the things you need during the day, like a rain layer, documents and snacks, in the tank bag or the top of a tail bag where you can reach them quickly.

body.h: Load the bike for good handling

body.p: Where the weight goes matters as much as how much there is. Heavy items should sit low and as close to the middle of the bike as possible, so put dense things like tools and shoes at the bottom of the saddlebags and keep the tail bag and top box for light, bulky clothing. Balance the weight evenly between left and right.

Check every strap after the first few miles, because loads settle once you start riding. Make sure nothing can touch the exhaust, the rear tyre or the chain, and that no loose strap ends can flap into the wheel.

body.h: Adjust the bike, not just the bags

body.p: Extra weight, especially with a passenger, changes how the bike behaves. Most owner's manuals list a higher tyre pressure for a loaded bike, and many bikes let you add rear preload to stop the back end sagging. Brakes will need a little more distance too, so leave bigger gaps on the road. Before you set off, run through your usual [pre-ride check](/blog/five-minute-pre-ride-check) with the bike fully loaded.

body.h: Plan around the bike as well as the route

body.p: A weekend trip can add a few hundred miles in two days, so it is worth knowing whether a service or chain adjustment is due before you leave. Our guides to [planning a trip you will enjoy](/blog/how-to-plan-a-motorcycle-trip) and [getting your bike ready for a long trip](/blog/get-your-motorcycle-ready-for-a-long-trip) cover the rest.
If you want to log your weekend away and see when your next service is due soon, MotoLog keeps your trips, mileage and service reminders in one place. You can get the app just below.

title: Motorcycle battery care: how to keep it charged and healthy
alt: A black bobber motorcycle parked in a dim underground garage under fluorescent lights
excerpt: A flat battery is one of the most common reasons a motorcycle will not start. Here is why bike batteries die, how to test yours, and how to make it last.

body.p: Few things spoil a planned ride faster than pressing the starter and hearing a weak click. Motorcycle batteries are small, they often sit unused for weeks, and many modern bikes draw a little power even when they are switched off. The good news is that most battery problems are avoidable with a few simple habits.

A car battery gets a long charge every time you drive, but a motorcycle often does short trips or sits in the garage between weekends. Alarms, immobilisers, clocks and ECUs all draw a small current around the clock, and over two or three weeks that is enough to drain a small battery. Cold weather makes things worse, because a cold battery delivers less power just when the engine needs more to turn over.
Batteries also wear out with age. Most last somewhere between three and five years, and every time one is run completely flat it loses some of its capacity for good.

body.h: Check it before it lets you down

body.p: A cheap digital multimeter tells you most of what you need to know. With the bike off and rested for a few hours, measure across the terminals:

ul: Around 12.6 to 12.8 volts means the battery is fully charged
Around 12.4 volts means it is about three-quarters charged and worth topping up
Below about 12.2 volts means it is low and should be charged soon
If it will not hold a charge for a day or two after charging, it is probably time for a new one

body.p: While you are there, look at the terminals. White or green crust on the connections can stop current flowing properly. Clean it off with a wire brush, tighten the bolts and add a thin smear of terminal grease. You can fold this into your [pre-ride check](/blog/five-minute-pre-ride-check) every few weeks.

The single best thing you can do for a motorcycle battery is connect it to a smart charger, sometimes called a battery tender or maintainer, whenever the bike will sit for more than a week or two. A smart charger brings the battery up to full and then holds it there without overcharging. Many come with a lead that you can leave permanently attached to the battery, so plugging in takes seconds. It is essential if you are [storing your bike for winter](/blog/how-to-store-your-motorcycle-for-winter).
Make sure the charger suits your battery type. Lithium batteries, which are increasingly common on newer bikes, need a charger with a lithium mode, and using the wrong setting can damage them.

Short trips of a few minutes use more charge to start the engine than the charging system can put back. If most of your riding is short hops, try to fit in a longer ride of half an hour or more every week or so, or put the bike on the charger afterwards.

Because batteries fade gradually, it is easy to forget how old yours is until it fails on a cold morning. Note the date you fit a new one, and treat a check of the battery as part of your regular [maintenance schedule](/blog/motorcycle-maintenance-schedule), alongside jobs like [changing the oil](/blog/how-often-change-motorcycle-oil).

title: How to choose motorcycle gloves
alt: A pair of black leather motorcycle gloves resting on a chrome speedometer and handlebars
excerpt: Your hands work the throttle, brakes and clutch, and they are usually the first thing to touch the ground in a fall. Here is how to pick gloves that protect them and still let you ride well.

body.p: Gloves are easy to treat as an afterthought, but your hands do more on a motorcycle than any other part of your body. They control the throttle, the front brake and the clutch, and in a fall they are almost always the first thing to hit the road. A good pair protects you, keeps you comfortable and lets you operate the controls precisely. A bad pair does none of those things well.

Look for gloves certified to EN 13594, the European standard for motorcycle gloves. Level 1 is the basic pass and Level 2 means better abrasion and impact performance; the label inside the cuff will tell you which. Beyond the label, check for:

ul: Hard or foam armour over the knuckles
Reinforced palm sliders, the part that usually touches the ground first
A secure closure at the wrist so the glove cannot come off in a slide
Double or hidden stitching on the seams, which is less likely to burst

body.p: A glove should be snug without pinching. With your fingers stretched out, the tips should just touch the ends of the glove, and when you make a fist there should be no tight spots across the knuckles. Try them on while holding a handlebar if the shop has one, or at least curl your hand around something of the same size. Leather will relax a little with use, so a pair that is slightly firm at first usually ends up fitting well, while a pair that is loose on day one only gets looser.

Fit also affects control. Thick, baggy gloves make it harder to feel the brake lever and to make small throttle adjustments. Do a few slow laps of a car park in new gloves before a longer ride, the same way you would when [practising low-speed control](/blog/five-riding-skills-to-practise-in-a-car-park).
Most riders who ride all year end up with at least two pairs, because no single glove works well in every season.

ul: Summer gloves are short-cuffed and vented, often leather with mesh panels, so your hands do not get sweaty and lose grip.
Winter gloves have insulation and a long gauntlet that seals over your jacket sleeve. They are warmer but bulkier, so expect slightly less feel at the levers.

Waterproof gloves use a membrane to keep rain out. They are worth having if you ride in the wet often, and they pair well with the techniques in our guide to [riding in the rain](/blog/how-to-ride-a-motorcycle-in-the-rain).

body.p: If you only buy one pair, choose a mid-weight leather glove with a gauntlet and good armour. It will cover most of the riding most people do.

Leather gloves last longer and stay supple if you clean them gently and apply a leather conditioner now and then. Let wet gloves dry naturally rather than on a radiator, which can crack the leather and shrink the fit. Check the stitching and closures as part of your [pre-ride check](/blog/five-minute-pre-ride-check), and replace gloves after a crash even if they look fine, the same as you would a [helmet](/blog/how-to-choose-a-motorcycle-helmet).

Good gloves are part of looking after yourself as well as your bike. If you want MotoLog to remind you when your bike's next service is due soon, and to keep track of your mileage and trips, you can get the app just below.

title: Motorcycle tyre care: pressure, tread and age
alt: Front wheel and tyre of a red motorcycle in motion on smooth asphalt
excerpt: Two small contact patches are all that hold your motorcycle to the road. Here is how to check tyre pressure, tread and age, and when it is time for a new pair.

body.p: Everything a motorcycle does, from braking to cornering to riding through a wet roundabout, happens through two contact patches roughly the size of your palm. Tyres are also one of the easiest parts to neglect, because they wear slowly and still look round and black long after they have stopped performing well. A few minutes of checking every week or two keeps them doing their job.

Motorcycle tyres lose air gradually, even without a puncture, and a tyre that is a few psi low makes the steering feel heavy, wears the edges faster and runs hotter. Check pressures at least every couple of weeks and before any longer ride, always with the tyres cold, before you have ridden more than a mile or two. Use your own gauge rather than a forecourt one, and set the pressures listed in your owner's manual or on the sticker on the swingarm or chain guard. Many manuals give a higher figure for riding with a passenger or luggage, so adjust for that too.

Most tyres have small wear indicator bars moulded into the bottom of the grooves, marked by a small triangle or the letters TWI on the sidewall. When the tread is level with those bars, the tyre is finished. Many riders change well before that point, because grip in the wet drops off noticeably as the grooves get shallow. Check the legal minimum where you live as well, since it is often higher than people expect.

While you are looking, check how the tyre is wearing. A flat strip down the middle of the rear is normal for a bike that does a lot of straight-line miles, but it makes the bike reluctant to lean. Uneven or stepped wear can point to wrong pressures or a suspension problem worth looking into.
Run your eyes and hand around both tyres and look for:

ul: Nails, screws or stones lodged in the tread
Cuts, bulges or blisters on the tread or sidewall
Fine cracks in the rubber, especially on the sidewalls
A tyre that keeps losing pressure faster than the other one

body.p: Anything that looks like a bulge or a deep cut means the tyre should be replaced, not ridden home and forgotten about.

Rubber hardens with time, even on a bike that sits in the garage most of the year. An old tyre with plenty of tread can still have far less grip than a new one. The manufacturing date is printed on the sidewall as a four-digit code after the letters DOT: the first two digits are the week and the last two are the year, so 2223 means week 22 of 2023. Many manufacturers suggest an inspection by a tyre specialist once a tyre is five years old and replacement by around ten years at the latest, whatever the tread looks like.

body.h: Make it part of your routine

body.p: The easiest way to stay on top of tyres is to tie the checks to things you already do. Check pressures each time you fill up, look over the tread when you clean [the chain](/blog/motorcycle-chain-maintenance), and note the mileage whenever you fit a new pair so you know roughly how long your tyres last on your bike and your roads.

title: How to ride a motorcycle in the rain
alt: Rider's view over the handlebars of a motorcycle on a wet, rain-soaked country road
excerpt: Rain does not have to end a ride. Smooth inputs, the right lines and a bike in good shape make wet roads far less stressful. Here is how to ride them with confidence.

body.p: Sooner or later every rider gets caught in the rain. Riding on wet roads is not dangerous in itself, but it leaves you much less margin for error. Grip is lower, braking distances are longer, and other drivers see you less easily. The good news is that a few habits make a big difference, and most of them are things you can practise on every ride.

In the dry, a tyre can forgive a rushed brake or a sudden handful of throttle. In the wet it often cannot. The aim is to ask the tyres for one thing at a time, gently. Roll the throttle on and off rather than snapping it, squeeze the brakes progressively instead of grabbing them, and finish most of your braking while the bike is upright, before you turn in. Steering should be calm and deliberate too, so set your speed early and keep the bike settled through the corner.

body.h: Leave more space and slow down earlier

body.p: Stopping distances on a wet road can easily double. Open the gap to the vehicle ahead to at least four seconds, and start slowing for junctions and bends sooner than you normally would. Extra space also gives you time to read the surface ahead, which matters more in the rain than almost anything else.

Some parts of the road lose far more grip than the tarmac around them when wet. Pick a line that keeps the tyres off them where you can, and stay upright and off the brakes when you have to cross one.

ul: Painted road markings, zebra crossings and arrows
Manhole covers, drain grates and metal plates
The oily strip in the centre of the lane, especially after the first rain in a while
Fallen leaves, mud and gravel washed out of field entrances
Standing water, which can hide potholes and cause aquaplaning

body.p: Rain and spray make you harder to spot, so wear something bright or reflective and ride with your lights on. Comfort is a safety issue as well. A rider who is cold and soaked loses concentration and gets tense on the bars, which is the opposite of the loose, smooth style the wet demands. Proper waterproofs, gloves that still grip when wet and an anti-fog visor or Pinlock insert are worth the money.

body.h: Your bike has to be ready too

body.p: Technique only works if the motorcycle holds up its end. Tyres are the most important part: worn tread clears much less water, and tyres that are underinflated or past their best lose grip early. Check pressures and tread depth regularly, not just when the forecast turns. Brakes need healthy pads and fresh fluid to stay progressive, and a [chain](/blog/motorcycle-chain-maintenance) that has just been through a wet ride wants cleaning and lubing before it starts to rust.

A wet ride is also a good reason to note what the bike went through. Logging the trip and the [mileage](/blog/why-track-motorcycle-mileage) tells you when tyres, chain and brakes are really due for a look, rather than leaving you to guess.

The best time to learn how your bike feels in the wet is on a quiet road with no pressure, not in heavy traffic on the way home. Take a short ride on a damp day, keep everything smooth, and build up gradually. Confidence in the rain comes from experience, and every calm wet ride adds to it.

If you want your tyres, brakes and chain ready for the wet season, MotoLog can remind you when each service is due soon or overdue and keep track of your mileage and trips. You can get the app just below.

title: Motorcycle brakes: when to replace pads and fluid
alt: Close-up of a motorcycle's front brake disc and caliper behind the fork leg
excerpt: Brakes wear slowly, so the change is easy to miss until it matters. Here is how to check your pads and fluid, and how often to replace them.

body.p: Brakes are the one system on a motorcycle you cannot afford to get wrong, and they are also the one that tells you least about its condition. Pads wear a fraction of a millimetre at a time, and brake fluid ages without any change you would notice on a normal ride. By the time the lever feels different, you are already overdue.

Most calipers let you see the pads from the side or from below with a torch. Look at the friction material between the backing plate and the disc. Many pads have a wear groove cut into the material; once the groove is gone, the pads are finished. As a rough guide, if there is less than about 2 mm of material left, replace them. Your service manual gives the exact minimum for your bike.
Check both front calipers and the rear. Fronts usually wear faster, but a rear that is used heavily in town or with a passenger can surprise you.

ul: A squeal or grinding noise when you brake.
The lever or pedal travels further than it used to, or feels spongy.
The bike pulls or the brakes judder under firm braking.
Scoring or a visible lip on the edge of the disc.
Brake fluid in the reservoir looks dark rather than light amber.

body.h: Brake fluid ages even when you don't ride

body.p: Most motorcycle brake fluid absorbs moisture from the air over time. Water in the fluid lowers its boiling point, so after a long descent or hard braking the fluid can boil and the lever can go soft. That is why manufacturers specify a fluid change by time, commonly every two years, regardless of how far you ride. If you can't remember when the fluid was last changed, assume it is due.

body.h: Discs and the rest of the system

body.p: Discs wear too, more slowly than pads. The minimum thickness is usually stamped on the disc itself. While you are looking, check the brake lines for cracks or bulges and make sure nothing is leaking around the caliper or master cylinder. Anything that looks wrong here is worth a professional opinion before your next ride.

Because brakes wear on two clocks, distance for pads and time for fluid, they are easy to lose track of. Note when you change pads with the odometer reading, and note the date of each fluid change. That record makes the next check obvious instead of a guess.

MotoLog lets you set [service intervals](/blog/motorcycle-service-intervals-cheat-sheet) by distance or by time and flags each one as due soon or overdue, which suits brakes perfectly. If you would like reminders for your pads and fluid, you can get the app just below.

title: How to get your motorcycle ready for a long trip
alt: A dark green motorcycle loaded with a tail bag and a helmet, parked on a dusty roadside
excerpt: A long ride puts more miles on your bike in a few days than it might see in a month. Here is what to check before you leave, so the trip is about the road and not the hard shoulder.

body.p: A multi-day trip is the best thing you can do on a motorcycle, and also the hardest thing you can ask of it. Hundreds of miles in a few days, extra weight from luggage, unfamiliar roads and no garage nearby. Most trip-ending problems are things that could have been spotted at home with an hour of preparation. A quick look over the bike, done a few days before you leave, also gives you time to order a part if something needs replacing.

body.h: Look at what is due before you go

body.p: Start with the bike's [service history](/blog/service-history-motorcycle-resale-value). Add the distance of your trip to the current odometer reading and see what that number crosses. If the oil change or a chain and sprocket check is due halfway through the trip, do it before you leave. Finding a workshop in a town you have never visited, on a day you planned to ride, is nobody's idea of a holiday.

ul: Tyres: check the tread depth across the whole width and the age of the tyres. A tyre that would last another month at home may not last two thousand miles.
Pressures: set them for the load you will carry. Your manual usually lists a higher figure for a passenger or luggage.
Chain: clean, lube and adjust it, and look for tight spots and hooked sprocket teeth.
Brakes: check pad thickness and fluid level, and make sure the lever and pedal feel firm.
Fluids and lights: top up the oil and coolant, and check every bulb, including the brake light.

body.p: Luggage changes how a bike handles. Keep heavy items low and close to the centre, and spread weight evenly across panniers. Adjust the rear preload if your suspension allows it, and take a short ride fully loaded before the trip so the first time you feel the difference is not on a mountain pass.

Bring the tool kit that came with the bike, a tyre plug kit with a way to reinflate, a few cable ties, some tape, a spare fuse and a small bottle of [chain](/blog/motorcycle-chain-maintenance) lube for longer trips. Save your breakdown cover number and a photo of your documents on your phone.

body.h: Keep a record as you ride

body.p: Note the odometer at the start and end of the trip and each day in between. You will know exactly how far you went, and when you get home you will know which services the trip pulled forward. Those miles count just as much as the commute, and they are easy to forget.

MotoLog makes that part simple: log the trip and its [mileage](/blog/why-track-motorcycle-mileage), and the app shows which services are due soon or overdue before you set off and when you get back. You can get it in the section just below.

title: The basic toolkit every rider should own
alt: An open socket set in a black case on a concrete garage floor, with a ratchet and loose sockets beside it
excerpt: You don't need a workshop to look after your bike. A small, well-chosen set of tools covers most of the jobs that keep it running well between services.

body.p: Plenty of riders leave every job to the dealer, and that is fine for the big services. But a lot of what keeps a motorcycle healthy is small, regular work: adjusting [the chain](/blog/motorcycle-chain-maintenance), checking tyre pressures, topping up fluids, tightening something that has worked loose. With a modest toolkit you can do all of that at home, in less time than it takes to book an appointment.

body.h: Start with what your bike actually uses

body.p: Before you buy anything, look at your bike. Note the sizes of the bolts you touch most often, such as the axle nut, the chain adjusters and the sump plug, and check the owner's manual for the torque figures. Buying the right sizes once is cheaper than a big generic set full of tools you never use.

ul: A socket set with a ratchet, covering the common sizes on your bike, plus a few extensions.
Combination spanners in the same sizes, for places a socket cannot reach.
A set of hex keys, and Torx bits if your bike uses them.
A torque wrench, so axle nuts, sump plugs and brake bolts go back to the right figure.
A good tyre pressure gauge. The one on a petrol station airline is not always accurate.
Chain cleaner, a soft brush and chain lube.
Nitrile gloves, rags and a drain pan for anything involving oil.

body.p: A paddock stand makes chain and wheel work far easier on bikes without a centre stand. A small battery maintenance charger keeps the battery healthy if the bike sits for weeks. A head torch and a magnetic pick-up tool will save your temper the first time a washer drops into the fairing.

body.h: Carry a small kit on the bike

body.p: For trips, a compact roll under the seat is worth its weight: the tool kit that came with the bike, a tyre plug kit with a few CO2 cartridges or a small pump, cable ties, a little tape and a spare fuse or two. It will not fix everything, but it turns plenty of roadside problems into a short stop instead of a recovery call.

body.h: Tools are only half of it

body.p: Doing your own small jobs is satisfying, but it is easy to lose track of what you did and when. Was the chain adjusted last month or last season? When did the oil go in? Writing it down each time, with the date and the odometer reading, gives you a proper [service history](/blog/service-history-motorcycle-resale-value) and tells you when the next job is due. That record is also exactly what a buyer wants to see when you sell.

If you would rather not keep that record in a notebook, MotoLog logs your services and [mileage](/blog/why-track-motorcycle-mileage) and flags each job as due soon or overdue, so your toolkit comes out at the right time. You can get the app just below.

title: How to store your motorcycle for winter
alt: A black sport motorcycle with a green frame resting on a paddock stand in a dark garage
excerpt: A few hours of preparation in autumn means a bike that starts first time in spring. Here is what to do before you park it up, and what to check when you bring it back.

body.p: When the days get short and the roads turn wet and salty, plenty of riders park the bike until spring. Done carelessly, that break can leave you with a flat battery, stale fuel and tyres with flat spots. Done well, it takes an afternoon and the bike is ready to go the first warm weekend of the year.

Road grime, salt and dead insects keep working on paint, alloy and chrome while the bike is parked. Give it a proper wash, dry it thoroughly, and pay attention to the wheels, the swingarm and the underside of the engine. A coat of wax or a protective spray on bare metal helps too. A clean bike also makes it easier to spot leaks over the winter.

body.h: Change the oil now, not in spring

body.p: Used oil carries acids and contaminants from combustion, and they sit against the inside of the engine for months if you leave them there. Changing the oil and filter before storage means the engine rests in clean oil. If an [oil change](/blog/how-often-change-motorcycle-oil) is close to due anyway, this is the obvious time to do it.

body.h: Look after the fuel and the battery

ul: Fill the tank close to full to reduce condensation, and add a fuel stabiliser if the bike will sit for more than a month or so. Run the engine briefly so treated fuel reaches the fuel system.
Connect the battery to a smart maintenance charger, or remove it and keep it somewhere cool and dry on a charger.
Check your manual for anything specific to your bike, such as draining a carburettor.

body.h: Take the weight off the tyres

body.p: Tyres that sit in one position for months can develop flat spots. Put the bike on a paddock stand or centre stand if you can, so one or both wheels are off the ground. If not, pump the tyres up to the recommended pressure and move the bike a little every few weeks.

body.h: Cover it and keep it dry

body.p: A garage or shed is ideal. Use a breathable cover rather than a plastic sheet, which traps moisture against the bike. If the bike has to stay outside, an outdoor cover that is designed to vent is worth the money. Plugging the exhaust outlets keeps out damp and small animals, as long as you remember to remove the plugs before you start it.

body.h: Write down where you left off

body.p: Before you walk away, record the date and the odometer reading, along with what you did: oil changed, battery on charge, fuel treated. It takes a minute, and in March it answers the question you will otherwise be guessing at. In MotoLog you can log the mileage and the services you did, and because [service intervals](/blog/motorcycle-service-intervals-cheat-sheet) can be set by time as well as distance, anything that falls due over the winter still shows up as due soon or overdue.

ul: Remove exhaust plugs and the cover, and refit the charged battery.
Check tyre pressures, chain tension and lubrication, and brake fluid level.
Look underneath for leaks and test the brakes before your first proper ride.
Check what services came due while the bike was parked.

body.p: An afternoon of preparation now saves you a dead battery and a frustrating first ride. Park it carefully, write down where you left off, and the bike will be ready when the roads are.

title: How often should you change your motorcycle's oil?
alt: A rider working on a motorcycle in a garage with a socket set laid out beside the bike
excerpt: Oil is the cheapest insurance your engine has. Here is how to work out the right interval for your bike, and how to stop it slipping past.

body.p: Engine oil does more than lubricate. It cools, cleans and protects everything inside the engine, and on most motorcycles it also looks after the clutch and gearbox. Old oil does all of that worse, which is why an oil change is the service most riders will do more often than any other.

body.h: Start with the manual, then adjust for how you ride

body.p: Your owner's manual gives a [service interval](/blog/motorcycle-service-intervals-cheat-sheet), usually as a distance, a time, or both, whichever comes first. That second part matters. A bike that only does a few hundred miles a year still needs fresh oil, because oil ages in the sump even when the bike is parked.

Then think about how you actually ride. Short trips that never fully warm the engine, stop-start city riding, hot weather, track days and heavy loads are all harder on oil than steady road miles. If that sounds like you, changing earlier than the maximum is a sensible habit.

ul: The oil on the dipstick or in the sight glass looks very dark or gritty.
The engine feels rougher or noisier than usual.
The gearbox is notchy or the clutch feels different.
You cannot remember when you last changed it.

body.p: That last one is the most common. Most missed services are not a decision to skip them. The date and the [mileage](/blog/why-track-motorcycle-mileage) just fade from memory.

Change the oil filter at the same time. A fresh filter holds the contaminants that fresh oil picks up, and the manual usually pairs the two. While the bike is on the stand, it is also a good moment to check the sump plug washer and look over [the chain](/blog/motorcycle-chain-maintenance) and tyres.

The easiest way to stay on schedule is to record each oil change when you do it: the date, the odometer reading and what you used. Then you always know what is coming. In MotoLog you set an interval by distance or time, and the app flags the service as due soon and then overdue, so it never depends on your memory.
Check your manual for the interval that applies to your bike, set it once, and let the reminders do the remembering.

title: Motorcycle chain maintenance: clean, lube and adjust
alt: A hand spraying lubricant onto a motorcycle chain
excerpt: A neglected chain wears out sprockets, costs power and can fail at the worst time. A few minutes of regular care keeps it quiet and safe.

body.p: On a chain-driven motorcycle, the chain is the last link between the engine and the road. It works hard, it is exposed to water and grit, and it tells you when it is unhappy: noise, rough running or a stiff, rusty look.
The good news is that chain care is quick, cheap and easy to do at home. The less good news is that it is also easy to put off.

Grit mixed with old lube forms a grinding paste that wears the chain and the sprockets. Use a chain brush and a cleaner that is safe for your chain type (check for O-ring or X-ring compatibility), wipe it down, and let it dry before you apply anything new.

Apply chain lube to the inside run of the chain while you slowly turn the rear wheel, so it gets thrown outwards and works into the rollers. Do it when the chain is warm from a ride, and let it sit before you head out so it does not fling off onto the wheel.

A chain that is too loose can jump the sprockets. One that is too tight strains the gearbox and wheel bearings. Your manual gives the correct slack measurement. Check it at the tightest point of the chain, because chains do not wear evenly.

Many riders lube roughly every few hundred miles and after riding in the rain, and clean when the chain looks dirty. Manuals vary, so use the interval for your own bike as a guide and adjust for your conditions: dust, salt and wet roads all call for more attention.

ul: Lube: little and often.
Clean: when it is dirty or before a long trip.
Slack check: regularly, and after any adjustment.
Replace the chain and sprockets as a set when they are worn.

body.h: Track it like any other service

body.p: Chain care is a perfect fit for distance-based reminders. In MotoLog you can set up a recurring chain clean and lube, so you see it flagged as due soon before it becomes overdue, and you can log it in a few seconds when it is done.

title: Why you should track your motorcycle's mileage
alt: Close-up of a motorcycle tachometer and instrument cluster
excerpt: Your odometer is more useful than it looks. Logging it regularly makes servicing, budgeting and resale easier.

body.p: Most riders glance at the odometer without thinking much about it. But the number is the backbone of nearly every maintenance decision: when oil is due, when [the chain](/blog/motorcycle-chain-maintenance) needs attention, when tyres and brake fluid should be looked at. If you do not know your mileage, you cannot know what is due.

[Service intervals](/blog/motorcycle-service-intervals-cheat-sheet) are usually written in distance, time, or both. Without a recent odometer reading you are guessing how far you are from the next one. A short log of readings, even just after rides, turns that guess into a clear number.

body.h: See how much you really ride

body.p: It is surprisingly common to be wrong about how much you ride. Some riders discover they cover far more than they thought, and need to service more often. Others find the bike sits idle, so time-based intervals matter more than distance. Tracking your distance per month and per year shows which one applies to you.

ul: Plan service and parts costs more accurately.
Spot a change in usage, like a new commute.
Know when a warranty or inspection limit is approaching.
Have an accurate figure ready when you sell.

body.p: You do not need a spreadsheet. Note the odometer at the end of a ride or whenever you fuel up, and let the numbers build up. The habit matters more than the method.
With MotoLog you log your odometer after a ride and see your distance per month and per year. Your service reminders then match how much you actually ride, instead of how much you think you ride.

title: The 5-minute pre-ride check every rider should do
alt: A rider in a black helmet and leathers on a mountain road
excerpt: A quick walk around the bike before you set off catches most problems while they are still small. Here is a simple routine you can repeat every time.

body.p: A motorcycle gives you less margin for error than a car, so a short check before you ride is time well spent. It takes about five minutes once it becomes a habit, and it catches the kind of small problems that turn into big ones at speed.

Check [tyre pressures](/blog/motorcycle-tyre-care-pressure-tread-and-age) with a gauge when the tyres are cold, and compare them to the figures in your manual. Look at the tread and sidewalls for cuts, bulges or embedded objects. Under-inflated tyres affect handling and wear faster.

Pull the brake and clutch levers and check they move smoothly and return fully. Press the brake pedal. Check that the throttle snaps closed when released. Look for fluid levels in the brake reservoirs and for any leaks around the calipers.
Switch on the ignition and check the headlight, brake light, indicators and horn. A bike that others cannot see or hear is a bike at risk.

ul: Chain: slack and lubrication, as per your manual.
Oil and coolant: levels at the correct marks.
Fuel: enough for the ride, with a margin.
Bolts and bags: nothing loose, luggage secure.

body.h: Make it a habit, then back it up

body.p: The pre-ride check catches what you can see today. The service schedule catches what you cannot: wear that builds up over distance and time. Used together they cover both. MotoLog keeps the second half in order by flagging each service as it comes due, so your walk-around only has to cover the first.
A few minutes before every ride is a small price for arriving where you meant to go.

title: How to plan a motorcycle trip you will actually enjoy
alt: A group of motorcyclists riding on a curving road lined with trees
excerpt: A good ride starts before you leave the driveway. Plan the route, the stops and the bike, and the trip takes care of itself.

body.p: The best motorcycle trips are rarely the most complicated. They are the ones where the route is comfortable, the stops are in the right places and the bike behaves. A little planning is what makes that possible.

body.h: Choose a route that suits the bike and the riders

body.p: Pick a start, a destination and a rough distance you will be happy to cover in a day. Be realistic: curvy roads, weather and photo stops all slow you down. If you ride with others, plan around the least experienced rider, not the fastest.

Know roughly how far your bike goes on a tank, and plan fuel stops with a margin, especially in remote areas. Build in a break every couple of hours. Tired riders make mistakes, and breaks make the ride more enjoyable anyway.

body.h: Check the bike before you go

body.p: Before a long trip, look at the things that matter most: tyres, brakes, oil, [chain](/blog/motorcycle-chain-maintenance), lights and coolant. Is a service due soon? It is much better to do it a week before the trip than to find out about it two hundred miles from home.

ul: Check what is due soon or overdue on your bike.
Look over tyres, brakes, fluids and chain.
Pack basic tools, a puncture repair kit and a phone charger.
Tell someone your route and rough timings.

body.h: Keep a record of the trip

body.p: Trips are worth remembering, and the distance counts towards your maintenance. In MotoLog you can map out your next ride with a start, a destination, dates and notes, mark it as ridden afterwards, and the distance goes straight into your log. That keeps your [mileage](/blog/why-track-motorcycle-mileage) accurate and your service reminders in step with what you really rode.
Plan the practical parts, then leave plenty of room for the unplanned ones. That is where the best stories come from.

title: A simple motorcycle maintenance schedule
alt: A rider working on a motorcycle in a garage with tools laid out beside the bike
excerpt: Oil, chain, tyres, brake fluid and more: what to look at, how often, and how to keep it all straight without a notebook.

body.p: Motorcycles are not complicated to look after, but there are a lot of small jobs, each with its own interval. Some are measured in distance, others in time, and it is easy to lose track of which is next.
Always follow the schedule in your own manual, since it varies by model. As a general guide, these are the areas most riders keep an eye on.

ul: Tyre pressure and condition.
Chain slack and lubrication.
Oil and coolant levels.
Lights, brakes and controls.
Engine oil and filter, by distance or time.
Air filter, inspected and replaced when dirty.
Spark plugs, at the interval your manual gives.
Brake pads, checked for wear.

body.p: Some things age even if the bike barely moves. [Brake fluid](/blog/motorcycle-brake-pads-and-fluid-when-to-replace) absorbs moisture over time, and coolant has a service life too. Manuals typically give these in years rather than miles, which is exactly the kind of thing that is easy to forget.

Valve clearances, [chain](/blog/motorcycle-chain-maintenance) and sprocket replacement, fork oil and tyre replacement come around less often, but they are significant. Having a record of the last time you did each one makes the next decision straightforward.

body.h: One place for all of it

body.p: The hard part is not knowing what to do. It is remembering when. In MotoLog you add each service with an interval by distance or time, and the app shows what is due soon and what is overdue. When you do the job, you log it, and the clock starts again.
Set up your list once, and it keeps working for you every ride after that.

title: How a service history helps your motorcycle sell for more
alt: A dark green café racer motorcycle parked in front of a roller shutter
excerpt: Buyers pay more for a bike they can trust. A clear record of services and mileage is one of the easiest ways to show that.

body.p: When someone buys a [used motorcycle](/blog/buying-a-used-motorcycle-checklist), they are buying the previous owner's habits as much as the machine. They cannot see how it was looked after, so they look for evidence.

ul: Regular oil changes with dates and mileage.
Evidence of major services done on time.
A believable odometer history.
Proof that wear items were replaced when needed.

body.p: A bike with a tidy history is easier to trust, and trust is what turns a hesitant buyer into one who accepts your asking price. A bike with no history raises questions, and buyers tend to answer those questions by offering less.

Receipts get lost and memories blur. A year or two later, you may struggle to say when [the chain](/blog/motorcycle-chain-maintenance) was last replaced or when the brake fluid was last changed. Recording each job at the time makes it simple to answer, and it makes it simple to show.

body.h: Good records help you ride, too

body.p: A service history is not just for the sale. It is the same information that keeps the bike reliable while you own it. Knowing what was done and when tells you what is coming next, and helps you catch problems earlier.

You do not have to wait for the day you sell. Every service you log today adds to the story. MotoLog keeps your services and [mileage](/blog/why-track-motorcycle-mileage) in one place on your phone, so when the time comes you have the history ready instead of a drawer of half-remembered receipts.
A well-kept bike is easier to enjoy and easier to sell. The records are how you prove it.

title: Buying a used motorcycle: the checklist to run before you pay
alt: A rider crouching beside a motorcycle in a garage, working on it with a toolkit open beside them
excerpt: A used bike is only a good deal if you know what you are buying. Here is what to ask, check and walk away from.

body.p: Buying used can save you a lot of money, but the price on the advert is only part of the story. What decides whether it is a good deal is how the bike was looked after. This checklist helps you find that out before you hand anything over.

ul: The seller's name matches the registration document.
The frame number on the bike matches the documents.
There is a service history, ideally with dates and mileage.
Any claims about previous owners or accidents are written down, not just promised.

body.p: If a seller cannot or will not show any records, treat that as information. It does not always mean the bike is bad, but it means you are taking their word for it.

Compare the odometer with the service records and the general wear. A low reading with worn pegs, a shiny seat and tired tyres does not add up. A believable history, with [mileage](/blog/why-track-motorcycle-mileage) rising steadily between services, is far more reassuring than a single round number.

body.h: Look at the bike with the engine cold

ul: Ask the seller not to warm it up before you arrive, so you can hear a cold start.
Look for oil or coolant weeping from the engine, forks and shocks.
Check the chain and sprockets: hooked teeth and a stiff or rusty chain mean money soon.
Read the date code on the tyres. Old rubber hardens even when the tread looks fine.
Squeeze the brake and clutch levers and check they feel smooth and consistent.

body.p: A short test ride tells you more than any photo. Listen for odd noises, notice whether it pulls to one side, and check it shifts cleanly through the gears. If the seller will not allow a ride, ask them why.

Worn tyres, an overdue service or a tired [chain](/blog/motorcycle-chain-maintenance) are all fair reasons to ask for a lower price, because you will have to pay for them. Point at the specific thing and what it costs, and the conversation stays calm.

Once the bike is yours, the first thing worth doing is writing down the mileage and the date, and then every service from there. It is the same evidence you just asked the seller for. MotoLog keeps your services and mileage in one place on your phone and flags what is due soon or overdue, so you always know where the bike stands.
Buy carefully, and the next owner, whether that is you in five years or someone else, will thank you for the records.

title: How to choose a motorcycle helmet that fits and lasts
alt: A motorcyclist checking their bike and gear before a ride
excerpt: The best helmet is the one that fits your head and gets worn every ride. Here is how to pick one and know when to replace it.

body.p: A helmet is the most important piece of kit you own, and a surprising amount of its protection depends on fit. A good helmet that does not fit is worse than a modest one that does.

Try helmets on in person if you can. It should feel snug all the way round, with the cheek pads firm against your face and no sharp pressure points, especially on your forehead. When you hold the chin bar and try to roll it forwards or sideways, your skin should move with the helmet instead of the helmet sliding over your head.

ul: Wear it for at least ten minutes in the shop. Hot spots show up with time.
Check you can see to the sides without turning the whole helmet.
Fasten the strap and make sure the helmet does not lift off when pulled from the back.

body.h: Look for a recognised safety standard

body.p: Helmets are tested to standards such as ECE 22.06, which is the current European one, or DOT in the United States. The sticker or label shows which one it meets. Check which standard applies where you ride, and be wary of helmets with no labelling at all.

body.h: Pick the style for how you ride

ul: Full face: the most coverage, and the usual choice for fast or long rides.
Modular: the chin bar flips up, handy for commuting and stops.
Open face: lighter and airier, with less protection for your face.
Adventure: a peak and a larger visor opening for mixed roads and trails.

body.p: Replace a helmet after any hard impact, even if it looks fine, because the protective liner may be damaged where you cannot see. Many manufacturers also advise replacing a helmet around five years after you start using it, as materials age. Check what the maker of yours recommends.

Clean the shell and visor with mild soap and water, and avoid strong solvents or stickers that can weaken the shell. Store it somewhere cool and dry and never hang it by its strap on a mirror, where it can get knocked.

It is easy to forget when you bought it. Note the purchase date somewhere you will see it again. If you already keep your rides and bike details in MotoLog, that is a natural place to keep a reminder of how long the helmet has been in use.
Choose well, replace when it is time, and wear it every ride.

title: Five riding skills to practise in an empty car park
alt: A motorcycle on an open road at the start of a journey
excerpt: You do not need a track day to ride better. A quiet car park and an hour is enough to build skills that matter on the road.

body.p: Most of us learn to ride well enough to pass a test and then stop practising. A quiet car park and an hour every few weeks can fix that. Here are five skills worth working on, in the order that usually helps most.

Squeeze the front brake smoothly instead of grabbing it, and add the rear as you slow. Practise from a low speed, building up gradually, until you can stop quickly in a straight line without the bike feeling twitchy. Hard stopping is a habit, so it is worth rehearsing before you ever need it.

Ride in a slow, tight circle using a little rear brake and the clutch friction zone, keeping your head up and looking where you want to go. This is the skill that makes junctions, filtering and parking feel easy.
Look over your shoulder to where you want to finish, keep the revs steady, drag a little rear brake and let the bike lean while you stay upright. Start wide, then slowly tighten the circle.
Set up some cones or markers and practise turning your head to the exit before you turn the bars. The bike follows your eyes. This habit carries straight onto real bends.

Practise rolling the throttle on and off gently and matching your shifts, so the bike never lurches. Smooth riding is safer and easier on [the chain](/blog/motorcycle-chain-maintenance), clutch and tyres.

ul: Pick one skill per session instead of trying everything.
Keep sessions short, about an hour, so you stay sharp.
Check your tyre pressures and chain before you go. A quick look takes minutes.
Find a place with no traffic, and ask permission if it is private.

body.p: If you log your rides and [mileage](/blog/why-track-motorcycle-mileage) in MotoLog, you will see how much you actually ride, and a practice session is a good reason to get out. Mileage between services and trips both build up over a season, and the app keeps them in one place.
Little and often beats one big effort. Your future self on a wet road will be glad you did.

title: Motorcycle service intervals: a plain-English cheat sheet
alt: A motorcycle being serviced in a workshop
excerpt: How often does a motorcycle really need servicing? Typical intervals for common jobs, and why your owner's manual always has the last word.

body.p: Service intervals vary a lot between models, so the single most reliable source is your owner's manual. Think of this guide as a map of what usually gets done and roughly how often, so you know what to look for and what to ask a mechanic about.

Most manufacturers set intervals by whichever comes first: a distance or a time. A bike that only does a few thousand miles a year still needs its oil and fluids changed, because they age even when parked.

ul: Engine oil and filter: often every 3,000 to 8,000 miles, or once a year. Check your manual, as modern engines vary.
Chain: clean and lubricate every few hundred miles and after wet rides, and check the tension regularly.
Tyre pressure: check weekly, and before any long ride.
Brake fluid: commonly every one to two years, because it absorbs moisture over time.
Coolant: usually every two to five years on liquid-cooled bikes.
Air filter: inspect at each service and replace when dirty, often every 6,000 to 12,000 miles.
Spark plugs and valve clearances: set by the manufacturer, and can range from several thousand miles to tens of thousands.
Sport bikes: often tighter intervals, especially for oil and consumables, if ridden hard.
Cruisers: usually relaxed intervals, with the chain or belt checked regularly.
Adventure bikes: dust, mud and weight mean chain, filters and tyres wear faster off the tarmac.
Commuters and scooters: lots of short trips and stop-start riding are hard on oil, so do not stretch intervals.
Off-road bikes: often measured in hours of running time, not miles.

body.h: Do not forget the time limit

body.p: It is easy to track mileage and forget the calendar. [Brake fluid](/blog/motorcycle-brake-pads-and-fluid-when-to-replace), coolant and oil all expire on a date as well as a distance, so a bike that sits in the garage can still be overdue.

Remembering every interval across every part is a lot. MotoLog lets you log each service and set an interval in miles and months, then shows what is due soon or overdue so nothing slips. You enter the numbers from your manual once, and the app does the counting.
Keep to the schedule, keep the records, and your bike will repay you with reliability and a better resale price.
